title: Trump: DHS: We tricked schools into un-enrolling hundreds of thousands of visa students
description_short: Trump: DHS: We tricked schools into un-enrolling hundreds of thousands of visa students
description_medium: The linked timeline quotes a DHS court filing stating that “terminating a record in SEVIS does not terminate an individual’s non-immigrant status.” It says hundreds of students’ records were ended, prompting some universities to remove students from enrollment even though the filing said the database action did not itself end their immigration status. The source does not identify the case or confirm a total.

title: Trump admin freezes billions in childcare, other social services against Democratic states
description_short: Trump admin freezes billions in childcare, other social services against Democratic states

title: Trump, Defiant After Bad Week, Pushes Ahead on Politically Unpopular Ideas
description_short: Trump, Defiant After Bad Week, Pushes Ahead on Politically Unpopular Ideas
description_medium: Trump, Defiant After Bad Week, Pushes Ahead on Politically Unpopular Ideas. President Trump continues to act like he’s politically all-powerful, even in the face of indications that he is not. This entry is cataloged as a standalone event because it captures a concrete action, public statement, legal development, documented relationship, or policy consequence linked directly or indirectly to Trump. The downstream effects include institutional stress, public-trust erosion, and accountability pressure across affected systems.
description_long: The Irish Times report described a week when Trump’s approval reached a second-term low, gas prices were rising, and Republicans in the Senate resisted two spending proposals. One was a $1.8 billion “Anti-Weaponization Fund” intended to compensate people who said they had been targeted by Democrats. Trump defended it publicly; senators questioned whether it could pay people convicted in connection with the January 6 Capitol attack. After Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche faced criticism at a meeting with Senate Republicans, party leaders scrapped planned votes on a separate $72 billion immigration enforcement bill. Trump also pressed for $1 billion in taxpayer funding for security at his proposed White House ballroom and attacked Senate parliamentarian Elizabeth MacDonough after she ruled that the funding approach violated Senate rules. The report’s “bad week” therefore refers to polling, inflation pressure, an unpopular Iran war and visible resistance from lawmakers in his own party. It presents Trump’s decision to keep pressing the proposals as a political choice to spend capital on his legacy despite those setbacks. The account documents the proposals and Republican pushback; it does not show that either spending plan ultimately passed.

title: Grocery Prices Rise in August 2025 as Analysts Estimate Tariff-Related Price Effects
description_short: Grocery Prices Rise in August 2025 as Analysts Estimate Tariff-Related Price Effects
description_medium: BLS data cited in the record show food-at-home prices rose 0.6% in August 2025 and 2.7% over the prior year, while coffee rose 20.9%. Yale Budget Lab separately estimated tariff-related food-price increases. The BLS figures do not attribute that month’s grocery inflation to tariffs, and the stored event date of April 5 predates the August data and their September release.
description_long: The record combines two different kinds of evidence. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that food-at-home prices rose 0.6% in August 2025 and 2.7% over the 12 months through August; coffee prices were up 20.9% year over year. Separately, Yale’s Budget Lab estimated that 2025 tariffs would raise food prices by roughly 3.3% to 3.4% in the short run and 2.8% to 2.9% over the longer run. Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller later cited staff research finding that tariffs accounted for much of the increase in core goods inflation. These analyses support discussion of tariff-related price pressure, but BLS did not attribute the August grocery increase to tariffs. The stored date for this entry is April 5, 2025, even though its central price observation concerns August and was released September 11. The description keeps the measured CPI result separate from estimates of tariff effects; it does not treat correlation as proof that tariffs caused the August increase. The event date and title’s causal wording need upstream correction before this record can be marked complete.

preserved_fields.title: Grocery Prices Rise in August 2025 as Analysts Estimate Tariff-Related Price Effects
preserved_fields.description_short: Grocery Prices Rise in August 2025 as Analysts Estimate Tariff-Related Price Effects

notes: The BLS archive URL returned HTTP 403, but the supplied source notes give the August CPI values and the September 11 release date. The title’s “tariff-driven” claim also exceeds what BLS reported; upstream date/title correction is still required.
